sample:
The quickest way to know whether writing works is to hear it.

Read a sentence out loud and the flabby parts announce themselves. A clause that runs too long makes you take a breath in the wrong place. A word you chose because it sounded clever turns out to be hard to say.

So paste something here. An article you saved and never finished. A draft of an email before you send it. A chapter you want to hear while you do the dishes. Cast a voice, set a rate that suits you, and follow the marker across the page.

content.footer: Aloud — text to speech, teleprompter and dictation. Runs in your browser.

blocks.p: Aloud is a free browser tool that does three jobs on one script. It reads your text out loud in any voice installed on your device, runs that same text as a scrolling teleprompter while you present, and takes dictation so you can write by speaking. Nothing to install, no account, no usage limit, because the speech engine is the one already built into your browser.

sections.h2: What is the difference between text to speech, read aloud and a teleprompter?

blocks.p: These get used interchangeably, but they are three different things, and the difference is simply who is doing the speaking.

cards.p: The machine speaks, you listen. Read-aloud adds a synced highlight so you can follow the words on screen while they are spoken. Good for proofreading, articles and accessibility.
You speak. The script scrolls at a pace you set so you can read while looking at the camera. No synthetic voice is involved. Good for videos, talks and pieces to camera.
You speak, the machine writes. Your words become the script, which you can then hear read back or run through the teleprompter. Good for drafting without typing.

blocks.p: They share one interface because they need the same things: a large legible script, a transport, a speed control and a position marker. In Aloud the script you dictate is the script the voice reads and the script the prompter scrolls.

ol: Put a script in. Type it, paste it, load the sample, or switch to DICTATE and speak it.
Pick your mode. LISTEN to be read to, PROMPT to read it yourself.
Set the pace. Rate and pitch in listen mode; words per minute and type size in prompt mode.
Press play. Scrub the waveform to jump to any word, or use the arrow keys. Space plays and pauses, Escape stops.

sections.h2: Does it work in my language?

blocks.p: Yes. Aloud reads any language you have a voice installed for, and the voice list is sorted so your own languages come first. Dictation listens in the language of the voice you cast.

Right-to-left scripts such as Arabic, Hebrew and Persian are laid out right-to-left. Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Thai are counted and paced by character rather than by word, because they are not written with spaces between words, and the teleprompter switches its dial from words per minute to characters per minute to match.

In listen and teleprompter modes, yes. The speech is generated on your own device by your browser and operating system. Nothing you paste is uploaded, stored or sent to a server, and the tool keeps working with the network off. Your script is saved in your own browser so a stray refresh does not lose it.

Dictation is the exception, and it is worth knowing. Chrome and Edge transcribe by streaming your microphone audio to their own speech servers. That is how the Web Speech Recognition API works in those browsers, not a choice Aloud makes. Do not dictate anything confidential.

If you are on a shared or public computer, switch off saving to this browser in the footer. Nothing is then written to storage and anything already saved is deleted. Otherwise the next person to open this page in the same browser profile would see your script.

sections.h2: What speed should a teleprompter run at?

blocks.p: Aloud defaults to 130 words per minute, a calm presenting pace. Conversational speech runs nearer 150 wpm and audiobook narration around 155. Rather than trust a number, read a paragraph out loud at the pace you actually want and adjust until the marker keeps up with you. Longer words are held longer, so the marker drifts the way real speech does instead of ticking like a metronome.

faq.a: Yes. Aloud is free and needs no account or installation. It uses the speech engine already built into your browser and operating system, so there is no usage limit and no API cost.

faq.q: Can I download the audio as an MP3?
faq.a: No. The browser speech engine plays audio directly and does not expose a recordable stream, so there is no file to save. Exporting audio requires a cloud text to speech service.

faq.q: How long can the text be?
faq.a: There is no fixed limit and nothing is trimmed. Long scripts are split into sentence-sized pieces internally, which also avoids a Chrome bug that cuts speech off after about fifteen seconds. Pasting a long script returns you to the first word, so you are not left staring at the bottom of your own text.

faq.q: Which browsers does Aloud work in?
faq.a: Text to speech works in Chrome, Edge, Safari and most modern browsers. The teleprompter works everywhere, since it needs no speech engine at all. Dictation relies on the Web Speech Recognition API and works in Chrome and Edge, and in recent versions of Safari.

faq.q: Why do I have more voices on one device than another?
faq.a: The voice list comes from your operating system, not from Aloud. macOS, Windows, Android and iOS each ship different voices, and you can install more in your system settings. Aloud sorts the natural-sounding ones to the top and lets you audition any of them before casting.

faq.q: Can it read languages other than English?
faq.a: Yes. Every voice installed on your device is listed with its language code, with your own languages grouped first. Cast a voice in that language and the script is read in it. The cast voice also sets the language dictation listens for.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.description: What Aloud does and does not collect. Text to speech and teleprompter run entirely on your device; dictation and advertising are the exceptions, and both are explained here.

blocks.p: This policy covers {{origin}} and every language version of it. It is written to be read, not to be survived.

blocks.note: Aloud has no server, no account and no database. The text you type or paste is never sent anywhere. Two things do leave your device, and only two: audio while you are dictating, and the ordinary requests any website receives. Both are set out below.

blocks.p: Your script, your chosen voice, your theme and your last mode are kept in your browser's localStorage. That is storage on your own computer. We cannot read it, it is never transmitted, and it does not follow you to another device or browser.
You can switch this off at any time with the saving to this browser control in the footer of the tool. Turning it off deletes what is already stored. Clearing your browser data removes it too.
We hold no accounts and no user database, because there is nothing to hold one in.

blocks.h2: Dictation sends audio to your browser's maker

blocks.p: When you use dictation, your browser transcribes speech using the Web Speech Recognition API. In Chrome and Edge that works by streaming microphone audio to Google's or Microsoft's own servers. This is how those browsers implement the feature; it is not a choice Aloud makes, and we never receive the audio or the transcript. Their handling of that audio is governed by their privacy policies, not ours.
Nothing is recorded while dictation is off, and the microphone is released the moment you stop. Do not dictate confidential material.

The site is served by Vercel. Like any web host, Vercel records ordinary request data such as IP address, time, page requested and user agent, in order to deliver the site and defend it from abuse. We do not combine those logs with anything else, and we cannot connect them to a person.

The typefaces are served from this site itself rather than from Google Fonts, so loading a page does not disclose your IP address to a font provider. Aside from hosting, the analytics described below, advertising where enabled, and the browser's own speech services, the site makes no third-party requests.

We use Google Analytics 4 to count visits and see which pages and languages are actually used. It records page views, approximate location derived from your IP address, device type and referring site. It never receives the text you type, paste or dictate, because that text never leaves your browser.
Google Analytics sets cookies to recognise a returning visit, and IP addresses are truncated before storage. What we see are counts, not people: we cannot identify you from any of it.
You can opt out of Google Analytics on every site with Google's browser add-on, or by declining in the consent prompt where one is shown.
Aloud sets no cookies of its own. Google Analytics does, and Google AdSense does where advertising is enabled. Both are described here.

If advertising is enabled on this site, it is served by Google AdSense. Google and its partners may then set cookies or read device identifiers to serve and measure ads, including personalised ads where you have consented. Google's use of advertising cookies is described in its advertising policies, and you can review or change your ad settings at My Ad Center.
Advertising never has access to the text you type, paste or dictate. That text stays in your browser.

blocks.h2: If you are in the EEA, the UK or Switzerland

blocks.p: If you are in one of those regions, analytics and advertising storage is switched off before the page loads and stays off unless you consent. This is enforced in the page itself using Google's consent mode, not merely promised. Where a consent prompt is shown you can change or withdraw that choice at any time from the privacy link it leaves on the page.

You have the right to ask what personal data we hold, to have it corrected or erased, to object to processing and to complain to your data protection authority. In practice we hold almost nothing: the honest answer to a data request is usually that the only data about you is in your own browser, where you can delete it yourself.
Aloud is not directed at children under 13 and we do not knowingly collect data from them.
If this policy changes materially, the effective date at the top changes with it.
Questions about this policy, or a data request: {{contactEmail}}.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.description: The terms for using Aloud. Short, because the service is simple: you bring the text, your browser does the speaking, and you keep everything you write.

blocks.p: By using {{origin}} you agree to these terms. If you do not, please do not use it.
Aloud is a free tool that reads text aloud, runs it as a teleprompter and transcribes dictation, using speech features already built into your browser. There is no account and no payment.

We claim no ownership of anything you type, paste or dictate. We do not receive it, so we could not use it even if we wanted to. You are responsible for having the right to use whatever text you put into it.

ul: Do not use Aloud to produce unlawful, harassing or deceptive material.
Do not attempt to disrupt the site or the infrastructure it runs on.
Do not present synthesised speech as a recording of a real person's voice in order to mislead.

blocks.p: Aloud is provided as it is, without warranty of any kind. The available voices, the quality of the speech and the accuracy of dictation come from your browser and operating system, and vary between devices and versions. We do not promise the site will be uninterrupted, error free, or suitable for any particular purpose.

blocks.note: Do not rely on Aloud as the only copy of anything. Your script is kept in your own browser and can be lost by clearing browser data, switching device or using private browsing. Use the download button for anything that matters.

blocks.p: To the extent the law allows, we are not liable for any indirect or consequential loss arising from your use of the site, including lost work, lost data or lost time. Nothing here limits liability that cannot be limited by law.

Dictation relies on speech recognition provided by your browser's maker, and where advertising is enabled it is provided by Google. Those services have their own terms, which you accept by using them.
These terms may change; the effective date above will change with them. Continuing to use the site means accepting the current version.

about.title: About Aloud
about.description: Why Aloud exists, who makes it, and how to get in touch. One script, three modes, built on the speech engine already in your browser.

blocks.p: Aloud began with a small annoyance: the quickest way to find out whether a piece of writing works is to hear it, and doing that on the web usually meant an account, a word quota and a card on file, for a job the browser can already do by itself.

Every browser ships a speech engine and a set of voices that most people never use. Aloud puts a proper interface on it, and then notices that three separate tools want exactly the same screen: a large legible script, a transport, a speed control and a position marker.

ul: Listen reads your text aloud, with a marker that follows the words as they are spoken.
Prompt turns the same text into a teleprompter and scrolls it at your pace while you read to camera.
Dictate reverses the direction: you speak, and your words become the script.

blocks.p: So the text you dictate is the text the voice reads and the text the prompter scrolls. That is the whole idea.

It is a static site with no back end. Speech, teleprompting and storage all happen in your browser, which is why it is free, why it has no limits, and why listening and prompting keep working with the network off. The typefaces are self-hosted so that opening a page tells no one anything.
The interface is available in English, Spanish, French, German, Arabic and Chinese, and the tool reads and dictates in any language your device has a voice for.

blocks.h2: What it deliberately does not do

blocks.p: It cannot export MP3s. The browser's speech engine plays audio directly and exposes no recordable stream, so there is genuinely no file to hand you. Doing that properly needs a paid cloud service, which would mean accounts and quotas, which is the thing this was built to avoid.
Bug reports, missing languages, or a voice that reads something oddly: {{contactEmail}}.
